title: Best PSU for RTX 5070 (2026): 6 Power Supplies Ranked
description: The Corsair RM750e is the best PSU for an RTX 5070: 750 W, ATX 3.1 and a 12V-2x6 cable. NVIDIA asks for 650 W; 6 PSUs ranked from $75 to $150.
dek: NVIDIA's 650 W figure is enough for most RTX 5070 builds. Here is what a typical build draws, when 750 W or 850 W is worth it, and the six units that fit.
intro: The Corsair RM750e is the best PSU for an RTX 5070: 750 W, 80 Plus Gold, ATX 3.1, fully modular and a native 12V-2x6 cable for $85–$100. NVIDIA lists 650 W of system power for the 250 W card, so the RM750e adds 100 W of margin for power spikes and a hotter CPU without paying for capacity you will never use.

This guide is for anyone building around an RTX 5070 or upgrading to one from an older card. Every pick is a Gold-rated, fully modular unit from a brand with a long power supply record. We cover how much power a typical 5070 build really draws, whether 650 W is enough, and when an 850 W unit makes sense.
quickAnswer: Buy the Corsair RM750e ($85–$100) for most RTX 5070 builds. The MSI MAG A750GL PCIE5 ($75–$95) is the cheapest good 750 W unit, and the be quiet! Pure Power 12 M 750W adds a 10-year warranty. If an RTX 5070 Ti or RTX 5080 upgrade is likely, buy 850 W now: the Corsair RM850e ($105–$130) or RM850x ($120–$150).

picks.label: Best Overall
picks.bestFor: most RTX 5070 builds with a 65–120 W CPU such as a Ryzen 7 9700X or 9800X3D
picks.skipIf: you already plan to move to an RTX 5080, which NVIDIA pairs with 850 W
writeup: The RTX 5070 is rated at 250 W, and NVIDIA lists 650 W as the required system power. The RM750e gives you 100 W more than that for $85–$100, which is the right amount of margin for this card: enough to absorb the short power spikes modern GPUs produce and to cover a 120 W CPU like the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, without spending on capacity a 250 W card will not use.

It is 80 Plus Gold, [ATX 3.1](/glossary/atx-3-1/) and fully modular, and it ships with a native 12V-2x6 cable. That matters because the Founders Edition and many partner RTX 5070 cards use the 16-pin connector, so the card plugs straight into the PSU with no adapter. If your card uses 8-pin plugs instead, the RM750e has standard PCIe cables too.

Corsair backs it with a 7-year warranty. Its 120 mm fan is smaller than the RM850x's 140 mm fan, but at the 400–450 W a typical RTX 5070 build draws while gaming it runs well inside its comfort zone. The direct comparison with the 850 W version is in [RM750e vs RM850e](/compare/corsair-rm750e-vs-corsair-rm850e/).

picks.label: Best Budget
picks.bestFor: budget RTX 5070 builds that want 750 W and a 16-pin cable for under $95
picks.skipIf: you want a long warranty or the quietest fan
writeup: The MSI MAG A750GL PCIE5 is often the cheapest good 750 W unit you can buy, at about $75–$95. It is 80 Plus Gold and fully modular, with a native 16-pin GPU cable that connects to a 16-pin RTX 5070 without the adapter from the box.

For a 250 W card it has the same 100 W margin over NVIDIA's guidance as the RM750e. What you give up is build quality at the edges: its fan and internal design are more basic, and MSI's warranty is shorter than Corsair's and be quiet!'s on the other 750 W picks.

Check that the listing says PCIE5. Older A750GL stock without that suffix lacks the native 16-pin cable, which is the main reason to buy this unit for an RTX 5070. The two budget favorites are compared in [RM750e vs MSI MAG A750GL PCIE5](/compare/corsair-rm750e-vs-msi-mag-a750gl-pcie5/).
cons: Older non-PCIE5 stock lacks the 16-pin cable

picks.label: Best Warranty at 750 W
picks.bestFor: quiet RTX 5070 builds that want a 10-year warranty without moving to 850 W
picks.skipIf: you want the lowest price at 750 W
writeup: be quiet! built its name on low noise, and the Pure Power 12 M 750W is a calm 750 W Gold unit with a native 16-pin GPU cable and a 10-year warranty for $95–$110. That warranty is the main thing it has over the RM750e, which carries seven years.

On an RTX 5070 the unit spends most of its life at around half load or less, which is where a well-tuned fan curve pays off. If your PC sits on a desk next to you, it is a sensible extra $10 over the RM750e.
Like every 750 W unit, it is sized for the 5070 and similar cards. It will also run an RTX 5070 Ti, which NVIDIA pairs with 750 W, but not with the headroom the 850 W picks below offer.
cons: Costs more than the cheapest 750 W Gold units

picks.label: Best for a Future Upgrade
picks.bestFor: RTX 5070 owners who expect to move to an RTX 5070 Ti or RTX 5080
picks.skipIf: the RTX 5070 is the card you plan to keep
writeup: An 850 W unit is more than an RTX 5070 needs, but it is the cheapest way to make your next graphics card a drop-in swap. NVIDIA pairs the RTX 5080 with 850 W, and the RM850e covers that at $105–$130, about $20 more than the RM750e.

It keeps the features that matter: ATX 3.1, full modularity, a native 12V-2x6 cable and a 7-year warranty. On a 5070 today it will run at a lower share of its capacity than a 750 W unit, which also tends to keep the fan slower.
Older stock may predate ATX 3.1, so check the listing. For the full RTX 5080 picture, see our [best PSU for RTX 5080](/best-psu-for-rtx-5080/) guide.

picks.label: Best Premium
picks.bestFor: high-end RTX 5070 builds that want the longest warranty and the quietest running
picks.skipIf: you want to keep the PSU budget under $100
writeup: The RM850x is the premium choice: 850 W, 80 Plus Gold, ATX 3.1, a native 12V-2x6 cable, a 140 mm fan that stops entirely at light loads and a 10-year warranty for $120–$150.

With an RTX 5070 it is overbuilt, and that is the point for some buyers. A typical 5070 gaming load uses roughly half its capacity, so it runs cool and quiet, and it will carry the PC through two or three graphics card generations.

If you are spending $550–$650 on the card and want the PSU to be the last part you think about, it is worth the extra $35–$50 over the RM750e. Its closest rival is covered in [RM850x vs Seasonic Focus GX-850](/compare/corsair-rm850x-vs-seasonic-focus-gx-850/).
cons: $35–$50 more than the RM750e for capacity a 5070 does not use

picks.label: Best Alternative 850 W
picks.bestFor: buyers who find it cheaper than the RM850x on the day
writeup: The Seasonic Focus GX-850 matches the RM850x on paper: 850 W, 80 Plus Gold, fully modular, a 12V-2x6 cable and a 10-year warranty. Seasonic's long record as a power supply maker is a large part of why the Focus GX is recommended so often.
Its hybrid fan mode keeps it silent at idle and light loads, which is where an RTX 5070 PC spends much of its time outside games. The fan is 120 mm rather than 140 mm.
Treat it and the RM850x as interchangeable for this card and buy whichever is cheaper. At $120–$140, it often is.

ranking.intro: These picks are based on manufacturer specifications, independent power supply reviews and owner reports. Nothing here was bench-tested by Enthusiast Review. Wattage guidance comes from NVIDIA's published 650 W required system power for the RTX 5070 and its 250 W total graphics power. Prices are street-price bands that move with sales.
criteria: At least NVIDIA's 650 W figure, with credit for a sensible 750 W margin rather than raw wattage.
A native 12V-2x6 or 16-pin cable avoids adapters on cards that use the 16-pin connector.
ATX 3.1 or 3.x units are designed for the short power spikes modern GPUs produce.
A longer warranty signals the maker's confidence in the unit.
A $550–$650 graphics card does not need a $150 PSU, so value counts.
ranking.why: The RM750e wins because it gives 100 W of margin over NVIDIA's 650 W figure, a native 12V-2x6 cable and ATX 3.1 for under $100.

mentions.text: The Corsair RM1000x is far more than an RTX 5070 needs. NVIDIA pairs 1,000 W with the RTX 5090, so buy it only if that card is in your plans. For a 5070 the extra $50 or more does nothing for stability or frame rates.

The Montech Century II 850W offers 850 W and a 10-year warranty for about $95–$115, but it is ATX 3.0 rather than 3.1 and Montech's power supply record is shorter. For a 5070 build, a 750 W Corsair or MSI unit costs less and is the safer buy.

sections.h: What Wattage PSU Do You Need for an RTX 5070?
body: You need at least a 650 W power supply for an RTX 5070, which is NVIDIA's required system power for the 250 W card. A quality 750 W unit is the better buy, since good 750 W Gold supplies cost little more than 650 W ones and give extra margin for spikes and a hot CPU.

The table below adds up a typical build. The figures are rated or typical gaming loads, not measurements; your exact numbers depend on the CPU, the partner card and what else is installed. The [PSU calculator](/tools/psu-calculator/) works it out for your parts.

sections.h: Is 650 W Enough for an RTX 5070?
body: Yes, for a quality ATX 3.x unit. 650 W is NVIDIA's own figure for the card, and a typical RTX 5070 build draws around 420–450 W while gaming, which leaves room for short spikes.

We still rank 750 W units first because the price gap between good 650 W and 750 W Gold supplies is often $10–$20. That small step buys more margin for a 120 W CPU, quieter running at the same load and the option of an RTX 5070 Ti later, which NVIDIA pairs with 750 W.

sections.h: Is 750 W or 850 W Better for an RTX 5070?
body: 750 W is the better match for the RTX 5070 itself. 850 W only pays off if you plan to upgrade to an RTX 5080 or a card in the same power class, or if you pair the 5070 with a high-power CPU such as a Core Ultra 7 265K running high power limits in long all-core work.

If you are unsure, compare the two cards you might own: the [RTX 5070 vs RTX 5070 Ti](/compare/rtx-5070-vs-rtx-5070-ti/) page covers the step up. The 5070 Ti is a 300 W card that NVIDIA pairs with 750 W; our [best PSU for RTX 5070 Ti](/best-psu-for-rtx-5070-ti/) guide covers it in detail.

sections.h: Does the RTX 5070 Use a 16-Pin Connector?
body: The Founders Edition and many partner RTX 5070 cards use one 16-pin [12V-2x6](/glossary/12v-2x6/) connector, while some partner models use standard 8-pin plugs. Check the product page of the exact card before you buy.

For a 16-pin card, a power supply with a native 12V-2x6 or 12VHPWR cable is the cleanest option, and every pick on this page has one. If you keep an older PSU, use the adapter from the box, run each 8-pin plug from its own PSU cable, and push the 16-pin end in until it is fully seated with no gap.

sections.h: RTX 5070 vs RX 9070 XT: Do They Need Different PSUs?
body: Yes, slightly. The RX 9070 XT is rated at 304 W, about 50 W more than the RTX 5070, and AMD's guidance for it is 750 W. A 750 W unit therefore covers either card, while a 650 W unit suits the 5070 but not the 9070 XT.

If you are still choosing between them, the [RTX 5070 vs RX 9070 XT](/compare/rtx-5070-vs-rx-9070-xt/) comparison covers performance and price, and the [best PSU for RX 9070 XT](/best-psu-for-rx-9070-xt/) guide covers the AMD card's power needs.

sections.h: Can You Reuse Your Old PSU for an RTX 5070?
body: Often, yes. A 650 W or larger unit from a reputable brand, under about five years old, with two separate 8-pin PCIe cables for the adapter, can run an RTX 5070. Replace it if it is older, unbranded, below 650 W, or came with a prebuilt PC and lists no maker.

Older pre-ATX 3 units are the main risk. Some can read a modern GPU's brief power spikes as a fault and shut down, which looks like a random reboot mid-game. Our [best power supply](/best-power-supply/) guide and [best PSU under $100](/best-psu-under-100/) list cover more units.

sections.h: Should You Pay for Platinum Efficiency?
body: No. At the 400–450 W a 5070 build draws while gaming, the difference between [80 Plus](/glossary/80-plus/) Gold and Platinum is a few watts at the wall, which takes years to repay the higher price. Spend the money on a trusted brand and a longer warranty instead.
Every pick here is Gold or equivalent, fully modular, and covered for seven to ten years.

mistakes: Buying 1,000 W for a 250 W card
An RTX 5070 build draws around 420–450 W in games. A 1,000 W unit costs $50 or more extra and does nothing for stability or frame rates unless an RTX 5090 is coming.
NVIDIA's figure for the RTX 5070 is 650 W. A cheap 550 W unit leaves little margin for spikes and a hot CPU, and it rules out any bigger card later.
If you use the 16-pin adapter, run each 8-pin plug from its own PSU cable. One cable with two ends concentrates the load and can cause instability.
Push the connector in until it clicks with no visible gap. A partly seated 16-pin plug is the most common cause of connector problems.
Buying the old A750GL by mistake
The MSI MAG A750GL is sold with and without the native 16-pin cable. Make sure the listing says PCIE5.
bottomLine: The Corsair RM750e is the best PSU for an RTX 5070 because it adds 100 W of margin over NVIDIA's 650 W figure, connects to 16-pin cards with a native 12V-2x6 cable and costs under $100. The MSI MAG A750GL PCIE5 is the cheapest good option and the be quiet! Pure Power 12 M 750W the one with a 10-year warranty. Choose the RM850e or RM850x only if an RTX 5070 Ti or RTX 5080 is likely to follow.

faqs.q: What PSU do I need for an RTX 5070?
faqs.a: NVIDIA lists 650 W of required system power for the RTX 5070. A quality 750 W Gold unit such as the Corsair RM750e is the better buy, because it costs little more and leaves room for power spikes and a hotter CPU.

faqs.q: Is 650 W enough for an RTX 5070?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is a quality ATX 3.x unit. A typical RTX 5070 build draws around 420–450 W while gaming, so 650 W covers it with margin. Choose 750 W if you have a high-power CPU or may upgrade the card.

faqs.q: Is 750 W overkill for an RTX 5070?
faqs.a: No. It is about 100 W more than NVIDIA asks for, which keeps the fan slower and covers short power spikes. Good 750 W Gold units often cost only $10–$20 more than 650 W ones.

faqs.q: What is the best PSU for an RTX 5070 and Ryzen 7 9800X3D?
faqs.a: The Corsair RM750e. The pair draws roughly 420–450 W while gaming, and the RM750e gives 750 W, ATX 3.1 and a native 12V-2x6 cable for $85–$100. Buy the RM850e instead if an RTX 5080 may follow.

faqs.q: Does the RTX 5070 need a 12V-2x6 cable?
faqs.a: Only if your card uses the 16-pin connector, as the Founders Edition and many partner cards do. A PSU with a native 12V-2x6 cable is cleanest; otherwise use the adapter from the box with separate 8-pin cables.

faqs.q: Is 550 W enough for an RTX 5070?
faqs.a: It is below NVIDIA's 650 W figure. A very efficient build might run, but you would have little margin for power spikes or a 120 W CPU, and no room to upgrade. Buy at least 650 W, ideally 750 W.

faqs.q: Do I need ATX 3.1 for an RTX 5070?
faqs.a: It is not required, but it is recommended. ATX 3.x units are designed for the short power spikes modern graphics cards produce, which can make some older units shut down under load.

faqs.q: Can an RTX 5070 PSU run an RTX 5070 Ti later?
faqs.a: A 750 W unit can, since NVIDIA pairs the RTX 5070 Ti with 750 W. A 650 W unit cannot meet that guidance. For an RTX 5080 later, buy 850 W now.
